heading: Pemmican, river water and soapstone
intro: nêhiyaw (Cree) and Métis families at Fort Edmonton, Dene water Guardians in the Peace-Athabasca Delta and Inuit carvers in the Arctic all work with the properties of matter. Their knowledge of mixing, separating and choosing materials sits alongside the science of this lab. These connections show some of what that looks like here in Edmonton, across Alberta and across Canada.

connections.title: pimîhkân: a mixture made at Fort Edmonton
connections.text: City Museum Edmonton says First Nations and Métis people made pemmican for generations, and that in 1833 most people at Fort Edmonton were making it. Poet and educator Naomi McIlwraith, who has Cree, Ojibwe, Scottish and English roots, writes the Cree name as pimîhkân. She learned to make it from Olive Modersohn, Alice Harkness and their sister Mariah at Fort Edmonton Park. Meat is dried and smoked on an akwâwân, a meat-drying rack, until it is brittle, then pounded to powder. Fat is boiled until the solid chunks separate, and the chunks are removed. Dried, crushed berries and the rendered fat are mixed in. The fat binds it together.

sources.title: Source of the Cree names pimîhkân and akwâwân, and the method: Naomi McIlwraith, kiyâm (Athabasca University Press, 2012), "How to Make Pemmican"
Athabasca University Press: kiyâm by Naomi McIlwraith (author background)
City Museum Edmonton: Tasting Pemmican, From Community to Commercial (2026)

peoples: Dene: Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation (K’ai Tailé Dené)
connections.title: Dene Guardians test the water of the Peace-Athabasca Delta
connections.text: The Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation call themselves the K’ai Tailé Dené, "people of the land of the willow." They signed Treaty 8 at Fort Chipewyan in 1899 and protect reserves on Lake Athabasca and the Athabasca Delta. In their Ni ho ghe di community based monitoring program, community members hired as Guardians sample water weekly at seven sites during the open water season. They track turbidity, total suspended solids (TSS) and total dissolved solids (TDS). Elders guide the training, and Indigenous Knowledge indicators are evaluated alongside the scientific results. The Nation says changes to water quality, water quantity and fish health are of great concern to the community.

sources.title: Source of the Dene name K’ai Tailé Dené: Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation, About Us
Source of the program name Ni ho ghe di: Government of Alberta Open Government, Oil Sands Monitoring work plan 2024/25, Ni ho ghe di: Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation Community Based Monitoring

connections.title: Soapstone and the qulliq
connections.text: Rosalina Naqitarvik and Geoff Rayner-Canham write that soapstone, a soft rock found in small deposits across the Arctic, has been essential to Inuit life. It can be carved into bowls known as qulliq. Filled with seal oil, the qulliq was the only source of heat, light and cooking. Its wick is pualunnguat, Arctic cottongrass, dried and rolled with seal fat. Soapstone is mostly the mineral talc, and its colour depends on impurities. It is bright apple green near Kinngait (Cape Dorset) and black and dark grey around Qamani'tuaq (Baker Lake). Naqitarvik writes that lighting and tending the qulliq is a way Inuit women pass down their ancestors' traditions.

sources.title: Source of the Inuktitut names qulliq and pualunnguat, and the place names Kinngait and Qamani'tuaq: Rosalina Naqitarvik and Geoff Rayner-Canham, "The Land Beneath our Feet: Inuit and the Rock Ages," Chem 13 News, Chemistry and Inuit Life and Culture (University of Waterloo, 2022)

try: Pimîhkân is made from dried meat, crushed berries and rendered fat. Is it a heterogeneous mixture or a solution? When the fat is boiled until the solid chunks separate and the chunks are taken out, which separation technique from Lesson 6 is that most like, and which property does it use?

The ACFN Guardians track total suspended solids and total dissolved solids in river water. If you poured a river sample through filter paper, which solids would stay on the paper and which would pass through? Use the words heterogeneous mixture and solution, and name the technique you would need to get the dissolved solids back.

Naqitarvik and Rayner-Canham say soapstone is mostly talc and that its colour depends on impurities. Is soapstone a pure substance or a mixture? Why is colour alone not enough to identify a material, and which other property from Lessons 3 and 4 could you measure on a soapstone sample?

review_flags: Existing lab and deck content: the only Indigenous reference I found is the lab footer "Edmonton, Treaty 6 territory." It is accurate but has no source. No other Indigenous content appears in the lab or the deck, so nothing unsourced needs fixing.

Names used and where they come from: pimîhkân and akwâwân (meat-drying rack) from Naomi McIlwraith's kiyâm (AU Press); nêhiyaw / nêhiyawêwin from City Museum Edmonton (which writes Nêhiyaw and nêhiyawêwin); K’ai Tailé Dené, "people of the land of the willow," from ACFN's own About Us page; Ni ho ghe di from the ACFN work plan on the Government of Alberta site (no English meaning is given, so I gave none); qulliq, pualunnguat (Arctic cottongrass), Kinngait and Qamani'tuaq from Naqitarvik and Rayner-Canham. Please confirm spellings, and whether you want an English meaning for Ni ho ghe di requested from ACFN before use.

Naomi McIlwraith's AU Press page describes her as having "a mixed Cree, Ojibwe, Scottish, and English inheritance." I wrote "Cree, Ojibwe, Scottish and English roots." Is that wording acceptable, or would you rather not mention her heritage at all? Her teachers (Olive Modersohn, Alice Harkness and Mariah, from Nipawin, Saskatchewan) are named in her book, but their nation is not, so I did not name one.

City Museum Edmonton's pemmican article also mentions Mitsoh, an Edmonton Indigenous-owned company (founder Ian Gladue, Bigstone Cree Nation per CBC), whose original name Pânsâwân is translated as "dry meat" by the museum and "thin sliced meat" by CBC. Because the two translations differ and it is a commercial business, I left it out. Add it as a present-day example?

The qulliq also has ceremonial use today (the source says it is a custom to light the qulliq before ceremonial events). I did not describe that. Would you like to invite an Inuk Knowledge Keeper, or check with a local Inuit organization in Edmonton, before this goes to students? A second Inuit-authored source (Jean Becker, Inuk, Nunatsiavut, University of Waterloo, 2024) gives a different word for the wick, suputi (cotton grass), reflecting a different dialect. I used only pualunnguat with its own source.

Rosalina Naqitarvik's Inuit identity is clear from her first-person account (lighting the qulliq with Elders, a qulliq from her grandmother, ceremonies in Arctic Bay) but the article does not state it in a byline. I therefore did not label her in the text. Please confirm.

The ACFN source is a funding work plan hosted by the Government of Alberta. It was written by ACFN's Dene Lands and Resource Management, so it is Nation-authored, but it is a technical document. The plan does not describe a filtration step: the link to filtration (TSS stays on filter paper, TDS passes through) is in the try prompt as general science, not as a claim about ACFN's methods. Is that acceptable?

Considered and not used: Writing-on-Stone / Áísínai'pi pictographs (mineral pigment) because none of the Alberta Parks or Parks Canada pages I read describe the pigment, and it is a sacred Blackfoot site; ochre and stone tool ideas because I found no well-sourced Indigenous-led material in this session.
